title: Anastomotic leak
subtitle: Suspect early, scan early, control the source

sources.org: International Study Group of Rectal Cancer (ISREC)
sources.title: Definition and grading of anastomotic leakage following anterior resection of the rectum
The management of intra-abdominal infections from a global perspective: 2017 WSES guidelines
Surviving Sepsis Campaign: international guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock 2021
Systematic review and meta-analysis of use of serum C-reactive protein levels to predict anastomotic leak after colorectal surgery

red_flags.text: Unexplained tachycardia, tachypnoea or new atrial fibrillation from day two to day seven after an anastomosis.
Pain that increases rather than settles, new peritonism, or an ileus that does not resolve.
Change in drain character: turbid, bilious, faeculent or enteric content, or gas in the drain.
New confusion, oliguria or rising oxygen requirement, which are often attributed to a chest infection or delirium.
A C-reactive protein that rises or fails to fall from day three onwards.

do_now.text: Go and see the patient. Full observations, abdomen, wound, drain and stoma, and a lactate.

If sepsis or septic shock is likely, start broad-spectrum antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms promptly, within one hour for possible septic shock, after blood cultures where this causes no delay.
Resuscitate with balanced crystalloid to perfusion targets, and start a vasopressor if hypotension persists.
Tell the operating surgeon and the consultant now, not at the morning round.

assess.text: Track early warning scores and organ dysfunction; deterioration on the trend matters more than any single value.
A low C-reactive protein on day three has a high negative predictive value for leak after colorectal surgery and supports safe discharge; a high value is a reason to look, not a diagnosis.
Exclude parallel diagnoses at the same visit: pulmonary embolism, myocardial injury, pneumonia. Do not let them become the comfortable explanation.
Grade the leak once found: ISREC grade A needs no change in management, grade B needs active intervention without re-laparotomy, grade C needs re-laparotomy.

investigate.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast, and rectal contrast for a low colorectal anastomosis, urgently after resuscitation has started.
Free gas alone early after laparotomy is expected; extraluminal contrast, gas around the anastomosis or a perianastomotic collection are what matter.
Blood cultures, lactate, FBC, U&E, CRP, and drain fluid for amylase or bilirubin when the type of leak is uncertain.
If the patient is too unstable to travel to the scanner, the answer is theatre, not a better scan.

resuscitate.text: Small contained leak in a stable patient: antibiotics, and percutaneous drainage of any accessible collection.
Low pelvic leak with a defunctioning stoma: drainage, sometimes transanal or endoscopic vacuum therapy in specialist units.
Nil by mouth for an upper GI leak with distal enteral or parenteral nutrition; early nutrition support for every significant leak.

definitive.text: Generalised peritonitis or septic shock: urgent re-laparotomy for source control, without delay for further optimisation.
In a vasopressor-dependent patient with faecal contamination, take down the colorectal anastomosis and form an end stoma rather than repairing it.
A small early leak in a stable patient with limited contamination may be managed by washout, drainage and a defunctioning loop ileostomy, preserving the anastomosis.
Small bowel anastomotic leak in an unstable patient: resect and exteriorise, or leave in discontinuity for a planned second look.
Short, defined antibiotic course after adequate source control.

escalate.text: Consultant surgeon at the first suspicion, and the operating surgeon whenever possible.
Critical care for organ dysfunction or vasopressor requirement.
Interventional radiology for drainage of accessible collections.
Honest communication with the patient and family, including the likelihood of a stoma and of critical care, before theatre.

notes: The leak that kills is the one that was attributed to something else for 24 hours: chest infection, fast atrial fibrillation, ileus, or anxiety.
Physiology decides the operation. Repair or re-anastomosis in a septic, vasopressor-dependent abdomen is how the second leak happens.
A falling drain output is not reassurance; a blocked or displaced drain shows nothing.
